summary: The Sound lab measures sound: a spectrogram, the spectrum with its loudest frequency, an oscilloscope and a level in dBFS, from the microphone's samples or from the tone generator's own signal, computed exactly as the speaker plays it. The measurements are real and tested on known tones; the sound pressure level in dB SPL is an uncalibrated estimate.

claims.claim: The spectrum's peak is the frequency of the tone being played or heard.
claims.how: A 4096-sample Hann-windowed FFT (the song landscape's), scaled so a full-scale sine reads 0 dB, with the peak refined by a parabola through the loudest bin and its neighbors.

sources.title: Spectrogram
sources.says: Windowing the signal and taking the squared magnitude of its short-time Fourier transform gives the spectrum at each moment.

claims.note: Within 0.5% from 100 Hz to 12 kHz; the in-page test checks 440 Hz, 3 kHz and a 1 kHz microphone signal.

claims.claim: A square wave has only odd harmonics, at 1/3, 1/5 … of the fundamental's amplitude.
claims.how: The generator's square wave is analyzed like any other sound; its spectrum shows lines at 3f and 5f about 9.5 and 14 dB down and none at 2f.

sources.title: Square wave
sources.says: An ideal square wave contains only odd-integer harmonic frequencies, the nth with amplitude 1/n of the fundamental.

claims.claim: Two tones close in frequency beat at the difference of their frequencies.
claims.how: The second tone adds to the first; the level and the spectrogram swell and fade |f1 − f2| times a second.

sources.title: Beat (acoustics)
sources.says: An interference pattern between two sounds of slightly different frequencies, perceived as a periodic variation in volume, the rate of which is the difference of the two frequencies.

claims.note: Two tones 3 Hz apart are closer than one bin of the spectrum (11.7 Hz), so they show as one peak that pulses, as they would on any analyzer of that resolution.

claims.claim: The level is the RMS of the last 50 ms in decibels below full scale (dBFS): a full-scale sine reads −3 dB.
claims.how: 20 log10 of the RMS of the samples.

sources.title: DBFS
sources.says: In the convention where the RMS value of a full-scale square wave is 0 dB, a sine wave cannot exist at a larger RMS value than −3 dB without clipping.

claims.claim: The dB SPL figure is about dBFS + 120.
claims.how: A typical digital MEMS microphone has a sensitivity of −26 dBFS at 94 dB SPL, so full scale is about 120 dB SPL. The Toy tab can change the 120.

sources.title: Understanding Microphone Sensitivity (Analog Dialogue 46-05)
sources.says: If a digital microphone's maximum SPL is 120 dB, its sensitivity is −26 dBFS (94 dB − 120 dB); typical MEMS sensitivity is −26 dBFS.

claims.note: Browsers and phones apply their own gain (the page turns off automatic gain control where the browser allows), so the figure is an estimate, labeled uncalibrated on screen.

claims.claim: The metronome clicks once a beat at the tempo set.
claims.how: Clicks are scheduled on the audio clock at (k + ½) × 60 / bpm seconds; the pendulum's angle is A sin(π t bpm / 60), one swing a beat.

sources.title: Metronome
sources.says: A device that produces a sound at a regular interval, set in beats per minute.

simplified: The click falls at each end of the pendulum's swing. A mechanical metronome's escapement ticks at a set angle of its swing, which differs from model to model.
The dB SPL figure is uncalibrated and unweighted (no A weighting).
The speaker's cone moves with the signal at the frame's moment, scaled up so it shows; at audio frequencies a real cone's motion is far too fast and small to see.

Screens show the generator's signal as computed here; the speaker plays the browser's oscillators, whose square and saw waves are band-limited (they differ only above the highest harmonic the sample rate can carry).
